definition.text: The ability of soil to support plant growth and give steady, good-quality crop yields.

facts.text: A fertile soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and is free of toxic substances.
Helpful properties include enough depth for roots, good drainage and aeration, organic-rich topsoil, and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0.
Irrigating with salty, alkaline or acidic water can strip useful salts or build up harmful ones, cutting fertility; about 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated.
Soil organic matter and fertility are significantly correlated.

definition.text: The three main plant nutrients added as fertilizer, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which are always listed in a fertilizer's analysis.

facts.text: Bioavailable phosphorus is the nutrient most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils.
A 10-10-15 fertilizer contains 10 percent nitrogen, 10 percent available phosphorus (P2O5) and 15 percent water-soluble potassium (K2O).
Inorganic fertilizers are more concentrated and immediately available to plants than organic ones.

definition.text: The loss of soil fertility when the things that make soil fertile are removed and not replaced.

facts.text: It leads to poor crop yields and is becoming a global problem.
Causes include overly intensive cultivation, over-tillage, overuse of nutrient inputs that mines the soil nutrient bank, and salinization.
Fertile soil is being depleted in many African farming regions, especially the Sahel under high population pressure.

title: Dark earths

definition.text: Dark, carbon-rich, highly fertile soils, many of them created or enriched by human soil management.

facts.text: Amazonian Dark Earth was created deliberately by Indigenous communities and contrasts sharply with the poor weathered soils around it.
In Ghana and Liberia, combining different wastes produces African Dark Earths rich in calcium, phosphorus and carbon.
The size of pre-1492 Amazonian societies, and Dark Earth's role in them, are continually debated.

contested_note: Scholars debate the size of pre-Columbian Amazonian societies and how far Dark Earth shaped them.

definition.text: The organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes, and substances they make.

facts.text: It improves soil structure, water retention, soil biodiversity, pollutant retention, pH buffering and nutrient cycling.
It raises fertility by holding nutrients on exchange sites and slowly releasing nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur as it mineralizes.
It is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so measured soil organic carbon often stands in for it.
Microbes decompose plant litter into minerals plants can absorb (mineralization), while part becomes stable humus.
Organic matter builds up where cold or wet conditions slow decomposers, and breaks down fast in hot, rainy tropical climates.
About 70% of global soil organic carbon lies below 20 cm depth.

definition.text: Organic matter that soil organisms have broken down to the point where it resists further decay.

facts.text: Humus is usually five percent of soil or less by volume, yet it is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture.
Its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times greater than that of clay on a dry-weight basis.
Humic substances are classed as fulvic acid, humic acid and humin, in order of rising molecular weight and resistance to microbes.

title: Soil carbon pool
article: Soil organic matter#Function in carbon cycling

definition.text: The large store of carbon held in the world's soils, a key part of the global carbon cycle.

facts.text: The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the 750-gigaton atmospheric pool and 4.5 times the 560-gigaton biotic pool.
Organic carbon, mostly as soil organic matter, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons; carbonates make up the rest.
Soil can act as a carbon sink through sequestration or a source through greenhouse gas emissions, depending on outside factors.

title: Mineral-associated organic matter
article: Soil organic matter#SOC distribution with depth

definition.text: Soil organic matter bound to mineral surfaces or locked in aggregates, which protects it from decomposers.

facts.text: It can persist for centuries, while particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only years to decades.
Mineral influences dominate deeper soil carbon, helping explain why more carbon is stored at depth.

definition.text: An ecosystem found on land, such as tundra, taiga, forest, grassland or desert.

facts.text: Land ecosystems differ from aquatic ones by having soil rather than water at the surface, and plants extending above it.
Water availability varies widely on land, and temperatures swing more by day and season than in water.
Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface.
Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets their conservation, restoration and sustainable use.
